## Education and class

There are various theories regarding how educational attainment affects people’s redistributive preferences. On the one hand, there are theories that view education as a source of resources that enhances the development of technical skills and/or critical thinking, leading individuals to become aware of structural problems and, as a result, to support the reduction of inequality [@becker_human_1993; @freire_pedagogia_2015; @schultz_investment_1961]. On the other hand, in cultural reproduction theories, education has been understood as a source of social inequalities, as it reproduces individuals’ living conditions, preventing opportunities for intergenerational social mobility and, consequently, perpetuating the stratified social order [@bourdieu_reproduccion_2019; @bowles_schooling_2011]. Within the framework of redistributive preferences, reproductionist notions are grounded in self-interest theory, whereby those with higher levels of education tend to exhibit attitudes that reflect a desire to protect their privileged social positions—which, in terms of attitudes, could be understood as an aversion to redistribution or support for market-based justice. Thus, education can be understood not only through its enlightening role in social life but also as a cog in the reproduction of inequalities in society.

Recent literature provides empirical support for these two theoretical approaches to education. For example, research by @nye_education_2026 found, in an analysis of 282 country-year combinations from various international surveys, that in 95% of cases, education was positively associated with market-oriented attitudes. Likewise, @vannoord_educationbased_2019 used data from 31 countries to show that education is widely understood as the basis for social stratification. Other studies have found that higher levels of education are associated with a greater preference for public investment [@busemeyer_inequality_2012] However, the results from @liu_does_2026 suggest that education does not fulfill a generalized function; rather, both the enlightening and the reproductionist roles exist but depend on the level of education, where in countries with low inequality, basic education is associated with reproductionist positions, while in secondary and tertiary education, the enlightening role stands out. 

Given the important role that education plays in shaping individuals’ attitudes toward inequality, this study proposes the following hypothesis: 

$H_{2}$: **Higher levels of education will be negatively associated with a preference for market-based justice in education.**

In addition to educational level, the literature has shown that social class is also an important factor in the study of attitudes toward inequality [@kulin_class_2013; @lindh_public_2015; @lindh_class_2020]. The evidence shows that higher social classes tend to support market-based distributive principles [@lindh_public_2015; @immergut_it_2020]. In this context, among higher-income social groups, there is a congruence between their attitudes and their individual outcomes—that is, a legitimization of the market as a distributor of rewards that serves as a justification for social status. However, @langsaether_more_2020 emphasizes the complexity of attitude formation beyond a mere expression of self-interest and points to the case of the self-employed, whose income and social security are similar to those of the working class but who share preferences with the upper classes. Based on the literature, the corresponding hypothesis is:

$H_{3}$: **Individuals from higher social classes are more likely to prefer market-based justice in education**
